fields.title: Isaiah
fields.subtitle: Yeshayahu, “The LORD saves”
fields.description: The grandest of the prophets, whose name means “The LORD saves”: sixty-six chapters that reach from the temple in Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. Isaiah sees the Lord high and lifted up and hears the seraphim cry “Holy, holy, holy”; he answers “Send me.” He warns kings who trust in armies instead of the Holy One of Israel, and promises a child called Immanuel, a son on David’s throne named Planner of Wonders and Ruler of Peace, and a shoot from Jesse’s stump. Then comes comfort for exiles — a road through the wilderness, a shepherd gathering the lambs, those who wait for the LORD taking on fresh strength — and the servant pierced for our rebellions, by whose welts we are healed, and at the last new heavens and a new earth. The prophet the New Testament quotes most, set out line by line as the poetry it mostly is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Isaiah?
qa.answer: The first and longest of the major prophets of the Old Testament, sixty-six chapters of prophecy, mostly in poetry. It falls into three movements: chapters 1–39, warnings and promises to Judah and Jerusalem in the time of the Assyrian empire, including Isaiah’s call (chapter 6), the promise of Immanuel and of a king on David’s throne (7–11) and the story of Hezekiah and the siege of Jerusalem (36–39); chapters 40–55, comfort for the exiles in Babylon and the songs of the servant of the LORD; and chapters 56–66, the hope of a renewed Zion and of new heavens and a new earth. No prophet is quoted more often in the New Testament.

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Isaiah, and when?
qa.answer: The book is “The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz” (1:1), a prophet in Jerusalem whose work ran from the year King Uzziah died, around 740 BC, through the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, to the Assyrian invasion of 701 BC and beyond. Jewish and Christian tradition received the whole book as his, foreseeing the exile and naming Cyrus by the Spirit of God, and many Christians still hold this view; the New Testament quotes every part of the book under Isaiah’s name. Many scholars think chapters 40–66 come from later prophets in Isaiah’s tradition who spoke to the exiles in Babylon and to those who returned, in the sixth century BC. Either way, the book is bound together by its themes and its name for God, “the Holy One of Israel”.

qa.question: What does Isaiah 7:14 mean?
qa.answer: It is the sign Isaiah gave to King Ahaz when Syria and northern Israel threatened Jerusalem: a young woman will give birth to a son and call him Immanuel, “God with us”, and before the child is old enough to choose good and evil, the two kings Ahaz feared will be gone (7:14–16). The Hebrew word means a young woman of marriageable age; the ancient Greek translation, made before the time of Christ, rendered it with a word that usually means “virgin”, and Matthew 1:22–23 quotes that form, seeing the sign fulfilled in the birth of Jesus to the virgin Mary. Christians have held different views of how far Isaiah himself foresaw that fulfilment, but agree with Matthew that the child whose name means “God with us” has come, and that the promise of a son on David’s throne in Isaiah 9:6–7 belongs to him.

qa.question: Who is the suffering servant in Isaiah 53?
qa.answer: Isaiah 52:13–53:12 is the last of four passages, often called the Servant Songs (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12), about a servant of the LORD who brings justice and salvation to the nations. In the last song the servant is despised and rejected, “pierced through” for the rebellions of others, silent like a lamb led to slaughter, and yet afterward “will make the many righteous” (53:5, 7, 11). Elsewhere in these chapters Israel is called God’s servant, and Jewish interpreters have often understood the servant as Israel, or a faithful remnant, suffering among the nations. The New Testament reads the songs as fulfilled in Jesus: Philip explains Isaiah 53 to the Ethiopian official as the good news about him (Acts 8:32–35), and Peter writes, “By the bruises he bore you have been healed” (1 Peter 2:24).

qa.question: What does “the Holy One of Israel” mean?
qa.answer: It is Isaiah’s favourite name for God, used some twenty-five times across the whole book and only a handful of times elsewhere in the Old Testament. It grows out of Isaiah’s vision in the temple, where the seraphim cry “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Armies!” (6:3). To be holy is to be set apart, utterly other and utterly pure; and yet this holy God has bound himself to one people as their own. In Isaiah the title carries both warning and comfort: Judah is judged for scorning the Holy One of Israel (1:4), and the exiles are told, “The Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer” (41:14).

Each line of the poetry is set on its own, and “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
And they kept calling to each other, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Armies! All that fills the earth is his glory.”

— Isaiah 6:3

Isaiah is the grandest of the prophets. Its sixty-six chapters range from the temple in Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, from the armies of Assyria to new heavens and a new earth. It holds some of the fiercest judgments in the Bible and some of its tenderest comfort. It gave the church the child whose name is Immanuel, the voice crying in the wilderness, the servant who was pierced for our rebellions, and the promise of a world where “None will hurt and none will destroy”. Jerome, who translated it into Latin, said Isaiah should be called an evangelist rather than a prophet, because he told the gospel of Christ so clearly.

No prophet is quoted more often in the New Testament. In Luke’s Gospel Jesus begins his ministry at Nazareth by reading from Isaiah, and the apostles reached for it again and again to explain who he was. And no book of the Bible has come down to us in an older complete copy: the Great Isaiah Scroll, found in a cave by the Dead Sea in 1947, was copied more than a century before the birth of Christ, and contains all sixty-six chapters.

“The LORD saves”

The prophet’s Hebrew name, Yeshayahu, means “The LORD saves” or “The LORD is salvation”, and salvation is the word that runs through his book. “Look, God is my salvation!” sings the redeemed people in chapter 12. “Turn toward me and be saved, every corner of the earth!” calls the LORD in chapter 45.

The opening verse tells us who Isaiah was: “The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz: what he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days when Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah were kings of Judah.” He lived in Jerusalem in the second half of the eighth century BC, had ready access to the royal court, and was married to a woman he calls “the prophetess”. He gave his sons names that were messages: Shear-jashub, “A remnant will return” (7:3; 10:21), and Maher-shalal-hash-baz, “Spoil hurries, plunder hastens” (8:1–4), a sign that Judah’s enemies, Damascus and Samaria, would soon be stripped bare. His call came “In the year King Uzziah died”, around 740 BC, and he was still prophesying in 701 BC, when Assyria besieged Jerusalem. A later Jewish tradition says he was put to death under Hezekiah’s son Manasseh.

Isaiah’s world

The great power of Isaiah’s day was Assyria. Its armies pressed west, and the small kingdoms of the region scrambled for safety. In the 730s BC the kings of Syria and of northern Israel tried to force Judah into an alliance against Assyria, and when King Ahaz refused they marched on Jerusalem (chapter 7). Ahaz turned to Assyria for help. In 722 BC Assyria destroyed northern Israel and its capital, Samaria. In 701 BC Sennacherib invaded Judah, “marched against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them” (36:1), and laid siege to Jerusalem; but the city was spared (chapters 36–37).

Behind Assyria, Isaiah saw another power rising. When envoys from Babylon came to King Hezekiah, Isaiah warned that everything in his palace would one day “be hauled off to Babylon” (39:6). From chapter 40 the book speaks to a people who are in that exile, comforting them, mocking the idols of Babylon, and naming the Persian king Cyrus, who would conquer Babylon in 539 BC and let the exiles go home, as the LORD’s “shepherd” and “anointed” (44:28; 45:1).

The shape of the book

Isaiah falls into three great movements:

  • Chapters 1–39, set mostly in Isaiah’s own lifetime: warnings to Judah and Jerusalem, Isaiah’s call, the promise of a child on David’s throne, oracles against the nations, and the story of Hezekiah and the Assyrian siege (36–39), which forms a bridge to what follows.
  • Chapters 40–55, words of comfort to the exiles in Babylon: the LORD is coming to lead them home through the desert, the idols are nothing, and a servant of the LORD will suffer and bring salvation to the ends of the earth.
  • Chapters 56–66, addressed to a people back in the land but still waiting: calls to true worship and justice, the glory of a renewed Zion, and the promise of new heavens and a new earth.

Christians hold different views of how the book came to be. Jewish and Christian tradition received it all as the work of Isaiah son of Amoz, who foresaw the exile and Cyrus by the Spirit of God, and many still hold that view; the New Testament quotes passages from every part of the book under Isaiah’s name. Many scholars think chapters 40–66 come from later prophets who stood in Isaiah’s tradition and spoke to the exile and the return. Whichever view readers take, the book is one book, bound together by its themes, its picture of Zion, and above all its name for God.

The vision in the temple

Isaiah tells of his call in chapter 6. “In the year King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and towering, and the hem of his robe filled the temple.” A king of Judah had died; the true King was on his throne. Seraphim, fiery beings with six wings, called to one another the words at the head of this introduction, and the doorways shook. Isaiah’s response was terror:

Then I said, “Woe to me! I am finished. My lips are unclean, and the people I live among have unclean lips, and with my own eyes I have looked on the King, the LORD of Armies!”

— Isaiah 6:5

A seraph took a burning coal from the altar and touched his lips: “Your guilt is removed, and atonement is made for your sin.” Only then came the question and the answer:

Then I heard the voice of the Lord asking, “Whom am I to send? Who will go on our behalf?” I answered, “I am ready. Send me.”

— Isaiah 6:8

The message he was given was hard: the people would hear and not understand, until the land lay desolate and only a stump was left. Jesus quoted these words to explain why many heard his parables without understanding (Matthew 13:14–15), and Paul quoted them at the very end of Acts. But the chapter ends with a seed of hope: “its stump is a holy seed.”

The Holy One of Israel

From that vision comes Isaiah’s favourite name for God, “the Holy One of Israel”. It appears some twenty-five times in Isaiah, in every part of the book, and only a handful of times in the rest of the Old Testament. The holy God is utterly other, high and lifted up, and yet he has bound himself to one people: he is Israel’s Holy One.

For Isaiah, that holiness demands trust. When Ahaz panicked at the armies of Syria and Israel, Isaiah met him at “the end of the water channel from the Upper Pool, on the road to the Fuller’s Field” (7:3) and told him, “If you do not hold firm in trust, you will not be held firm” (7:9). Ahaz trusted Assyria instead. Years later, the Assyrian commander stood at exactly the same spot (36:2) to demand Jerusalem’s surrender. This time King Hezekiah took the enemy’s letter into the temple, “opened it out in the presence of the LORD” (37:14), and prayed; and the city was saved. The lesson is summed up in one of Isaiah’s great sayings: “Your strength lies in staying calm and trusting” (30:15).

Justice, judgment and mercy

Isaiah begins not with comfort but with an accusation. The heavens and the earth are called to listen: the LORD raised children, “but they have rebelled against me” (1:2). Their worship is busy and empty, their hands are full of blood, and the LORD is weary of their sacrifices. What he wants is plain: “Learn to do good. Go after justice. Set the oppressor straight. Give the fatherless child a fair hearing; stand up for the widow in court” (1:17). And then, in the middle of the indictment, comes an invitation:

Come, let us take this matter to court together, says the LORD. Your sins may be scarlet, yet they will turn white as snow; though they are as red as crimson dye, they will be like undyed wool.

— Isaiah 1:18

In chapter 5 Isaiah sings a love song about a vineyard that its owner tended with every care, which still produced only rotten grapes. The vineyard is Israel. The song ends with a play on words that is lost in translation: the LORD looked for mishpat, justice, and found mispah, bloodshed; for tsedaqah, righteousness, and heard tse‘aqah, a cry. Later the book will say that the fast God chooses is to “loose the bonds that wickedness has tied” and “to break your bread with someone who is hungry” (58:6–7). Holiness, in Isaiah, always has to do with how the weak are treated.

The child and the king

When Ahaz refused to ask for a sign, Isaiah gave him one anyway:

Because of this, the Lord himself will give all of you a sign: see, the young woman is pregnant; she will give birth to a son and call him by the name Immanuel.

— Isaiah 7:14

The sign was for Ahaz’s own day: before the child was old enough to know good from evil, the two kings he feared would be gone (7:16). But the promise of a child does not stop there. Two chapters later the darkness lifts over Galilee, “The people walking in the dark have seen a great light” (9:2), and the reason is a birth:

For a child has been born for us, a son has been given to us, and the right to rule rests on his shoulders. He has been named Planner of Wonders, God the Mighty Warrior, Father for All Time, Ruler of Peace.

— Isaiah 9:6

Chapter 11 adds that “A shoot will grow from Jesse’s stump”, a new David from the felled tree of David’s line, on whom the Spirit of the LORD will rest, who will judge the poor with justice, and in whose kingdom “The wolf will stay as a guest with the lamb” (11:6).

Matthew’s Gospel reads Isaiah 7:14 as fulfilled in the birth of Jesus to the virgin Mary, quoting it in the ancient Greek translation, which renders the Hebrew word for “young woman” with a word that usually means “virgin”. Readers have long discussed whether Isaiah himself foresaw a virgin birth, or whether God’s promise was larger than the prophet knew. Christians agree with Matthew that the child whose name means “God is with us” has come, and that the names of chapter 9 belong to him.

The mountain of the LORD

Isaiah’s hope is never for Israel alone. In chapter 2 the nations stream to Jerusalem to learn God’s ways:

He will be judge between the nations and settle the cases of many peoples. They will hammer their swords into plow blades and their spears into knives for pruning. No nation will raise the sword against another, and they will no longer learn how to wage war.

— Isaiah 2:4

In chapter 25 the LORD spreads a feast on his mountain “for all the peoples”, and does what no one else can do: “He will swallow up death for all time. The Lord GOD will wipe every face clean of tears” (25:8). Paul quotes those words when he writes of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:54), and Revelation echoes them in its last vision (Revelation 21:4).

“Bring comfort, bring comfort”

Chapter 40 opens a new movement with words that have been set to music more often than almost any in the Bible:

Bring comfort, bring comfort to my people, says your God. Speak to the heart of Jerusalem and call out to her that her time of forced labor is finished, that the penalty for her guilt has been paid, that she has received from the LORD’s hand double for all her sins.

— Isaiah 40:1–2

A voice calls for a road to be built in the wilderness for the LORD, the voice that all four Gospels hear in John the Baptist. People wither like grass, “but the word of our God holds firm for all time” (40:8). The God who measures the seas in his hand comes “Like a shepherd” and gathers the lambs in his arms (40:11). And the chapter ends with one of the best-loved promises in Scripture:

But those who wait for the LORD will take on fresh strength. They will climb high on outspread wings like eagles. They will run and not wear out; they will walk and not tire.

— Isaiah 40:31

Chapters 40–48 also mount the Bible’s sharpest attack on idolatry. A man cuts down a tree, warms himself with half of it and bakes his bread, and “What is left he makes into a god” (44:17). Against such gods the LORD speaks: “I am the first and I am the last; there is no god but me” (44:6). And because there is only one God, his salvation is for everyone: “to me every knee will bow” (45:23), words Paul applies to Jesus (Philippians 2:10–11).

The servant of the LORD

In these chapters a figure appears called the servant of the LORD. Sometimes the servant is plainly Israel: “But you, Israel, are my servant” (41:8). Yet in four passages, often called the Servant Songs (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12), the servant is one who has a mission to Israel as well as to the nations. He is gentle: “He will not snap off a split reed or smother a wick that is barely burning” (42:3). He is a light for the nations, “so that you may be my salvation to the farthest edge of the earth” (49:6). He is beaten and spat upon and does not turn away (50:6). And in the last song he dies for others:

But it was for our rebellions that he was pierced through, for our guilt that he was crushed. On him fell the discipline that won our peace, and his welts have brought us healing. Every one of us has wandered off like sheep; we have each turned aside down our own path, and the LORD has made all our guilt fall on him.

— Isaiah 53:5–6

He goes silent like a lamb to the slaughter, is buried, and yet afterward “he will see, and he will have his fill” and “make the many righteous” (53:11).

Who is this servant? An Ethiopian official reading this chapter in his chariot asked the same question: “who is the prophet talking about here? Is he speaking of himself, or of another person?” (Acts 8:34). Jewish interpreters have often understood the servant as Israel, or a faithful remnant within Israel, suffering among the nations. Philip, “Starting from that very Scripture,” told the official about Jesus (Acts 8:35), and the church has always read Isaiah 53 as the clearest picture in the Old Testament of the cross. Matthew applies the first song to Jesus (Matthew 12:18–21); Peter writes, “By the bruises he bore you have been healed” (1 Peter 2:24).

New heavens and a new earth

The last chapters widen the invitation again. “Listen, all who thirst: come down to the water!” (55:1). “Rise up and shine, for your light has come” (60:1). In chapter 61 an anointed messenger announces good news to the lowly and freedom for captives. In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read that passage aloud, stopped in the middle of a sentence before “a day when our God takes vengeance”, rolled up the scroll and said, “Today, as you have been listening, these words of Scripture have come true” (Luke 4:21).

And at the end Isaiah’s vision reaches as far as any in the Old Testament:

Look, I am about to create new heavens and a new earth. The things of the past will not be remembered; no one will even think of them again.

— Isaiah 65:17

Yet the book does not end with a garden. Its last verse looks out on the bodies of those who rebelled, whose “worm will not die” (66:24), the words Jesus used for the final judgment (Mark 9:48). Isaiah holds together what we are tempted to separate: the holiness that judges and the love that saves. In the synagogue, by long custom, the verse before the last is read again at the end, so that the book closes on all humanity coming to worship.

How to read Isaiah

  • Read it in its three movements. Chapters 1–39, 40–55 and 56–66 each have their own voice. Many readers begin with 40–55.
  • Keep the history close. The stories of Ahaz and Hezekiah in 2 Kings 16–20 make chapters 7–12 and 36–39 come alive; chapters 36–39 are told almost word for word in 2 Kings 18–20.
  • Read the poetry aloud. Isaiah is one of the great poets of the world, and his book is meant to be heard.
  • Watch for the threads. The Holy One of Israel, Zion, the highway in the wilderness, the nations streaming to the light, the remnant, the servant.
  • Read it with the New Testament open. Follow the passages the Gospels and the apostles quote, and see how they read them.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Most of Isaiah is poetry, and this edition prints each line of the poetry on its own, as the Hebrew sets it out; the stories of chapters 36–39 are printed as prose. A few of its choices are worth knowing before you begin.

“The LORD of Armies.” LORD in capitals stands for God’s personal name, YHWH. Isaiah’s favourite title for God, older Bibles’ “the LORD of hosts”, is rendered “the LORD of Armies”: the hosts are the armies of heaven. Where the Hebrew joins the word “Lord” to God’s name, it reads “the Lord GOD”.

The names of the child. In 9:6 each of the four names is translated by what it means: “Planner of Wonders, God the Mighty Warrior, Father for All Time, Ruler of Peace”, rather than the familiar “Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace”.

“The young woman.” In 7:14 the Hebrew word for a young woman of marriageable age is translated “the young woman”, with a note on the Greek translation’s “virgin” and Matthew’s use of it.

Numbering. The Hebrew numbers the verses of chapter 9 one behind most English Bibles, and those of chapter 64 as well. The references in this edition follow the English numbering.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Isaiah 1
fields.body_html:
Children who rebelled

1The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz: what he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days when Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah were kings of Judah.
2Listen, heavens; earth, open your ears,
for the LORD has spoken:
I raised children and made them great,
but they have rebelled against me.
3An ox recognizes its owner,
a donkey the feeding trough of its master;
but Israel does not know,
my people give it no thought.
4Woe to a nation that sins, a people loaded down with guilt,
the offspring of wrongdoers, children bent on corruption!
They have left the LORD, they have scorned the Holy One of Israel, they have turned away from him and gone backward.
5Where else can you be struck, as you go on rebelling?
The head is sick all over; the heart is weak through and through.
6There is no healthy spot from the bottom of the foot up to the head:
bruises, stripes, wounds still raw.
No one has squeezed them clean, no one has bound them,
no one has eased them with oil.
7Your country lies in ruins,
your towns are burned down;
foreigners eat up your fields while you watch,
and it is ruined like a land that foreigners have torn down.
8Daughter Zion is left like a shelter among the vines,
like a hut in a cucumber patch, like a town shut in by siege.
9Had the LORD of Armies not let a few of us survive,
we would have shared the fate of Sodom;
Gomorrah’s end would have been ours.

Sacrifices that give no pleasure

10Rulers of Sodom, hear the word of the LORD!
People of Gomorrah, open your ears to the instruction of our God!
11What use to me are all your sacrifices? says the LORD.
I have had all I want of burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fattened beasts;
the blood of bulls and lambs and goats gives me no pleasure.
12You come to stand in my presence;
but who told you to do this, to tread down my courtyards?
13Bring no more empty gifts;
to me the smoke of incense is loathsome.
New moon, Sabbath, the call to assemble:
wrongdoing and holy gatherings together are more than I can bear.
14Your new moons and your fixed feasts are hateful to me, to the depths of my soul;
they lie on me like a heavy load,
and I am tired of carrying it.
15Spread out your palms, and I will hide my eyes from you;
pile up prayer upon prayer, and I will not be listening.
Blood fills your hands.
16Wash, and be clean again!
Clear your wicked deeds away from before my eyes.
Put an end to evil.
17Learn to do good. Go after justice. Set the oppressor straight.
Give the fatherless child a fair hearing; stand up for the widow in court.

18Come, let us take this matter to court together, says the LORD.
Your sins may be scarlet, yet they will turn white as snow;
though they are as red as crimson dye, they will be like undyed wool.
19If you consent and listen to me,
you will eat the rich produce of the land.
20But if you say no and rebel,
the sword will eat you up;
for the mouth of the LORD has spoken.

The faithful town gone astray

21How the faithful town has turned prostitute!
Justice filled her once; righteousness made its home in her. Now it is murderers.
22Your silver has turned to slag;
your wine is cut with water.
23Your leaders are in revolt and keep company with thieves.
All of them love a bribe and go hunting for payoffs.
The fatherless get no justice from them;
the widow’s lawsuit is never heard in their court.

24So the Lord GOD of Armies, the Mighty One of Israel, declares:
Woe to my foes! I will be rid of them at last;
I will pay back my enemies.
25I will turn my hand against you;
I will melt away your slag as with lye and clear out all your impure metal.
26I will give you back judges like those you had at first,
and counselors like those at the start.
Then you will be called the City of Righteousness, the Faithful Town.
27Justice will set Zion free,
and righteousness will free those of her people who turn back.
28Rebels and sinners alike will be crushed,
and all who walk away from the LORD will be finished.
29Yes, the oaks you set your heart on will bring you shame;
the gardens you chose will make you blush.
30You yourselves will be like an oak whose leaves are drying up,
like a garden left without water.
31Whoever is strong will become tinder, and what he has made will be the spark;
the two will burn together, and there will be no one to put out the flames.
fields.summary: Isaiah’s vision begins with God’s charge against Judah, children who have rebelled. God takes no pleasure in their sacrifices while their hands are full of blood, and calls them to learn to do good and be made clean.

fields.title: Isaiah 2
fields.body_html:
The mountain of the house of the LORD

1This is the word that Isaiah son of Amoz saw about Judah and Jerusalem.
2In days to come, the mountain of the LORD’s house will stand firm, the chief of all the mountains,
rising high above the hills,
and the nations will all stream toward it.
3Peoples in great numbers will set out, saying, “Come, let us climb to the mountain of the LORD, up to the house of Jacob’s God,
so that he may show us his ways and we may walk on his paths.”
For instruction will go out from Zion,
and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.
4He will be judge between the nations and settle the cases of many peoples.
They will hammer their swords into plow blades and their spears into knives for pruning.
No nation will raise the sword against another,
and they will no longer learn how to wage war.

5House of Jacob, come!
Let us walk by the light of the LORD.
6For you have cast off your people, the house of Jacob,
because they are crowded with what comes from the east and with soothsayers, as the Philistines are,
and they strike hands with the sons of foreigners.
7Silver and gold fill their land,
and their treasures are beyond counting;
horses fill their land,
and their chariots are beyond counting.
8Idols fill their land too.
They worship things their own hands produced, objects shaped by their own fingers.
9So humankind sinks low, and each person is put down.
Do not pardon them!
10Get into the rocks! Bury yourself in the dust,
away from the dread of the LORD and from his majestic splendor!
11The arrogant gaze of humankind will be lowered,
people’s lofty pride will be bent down,
and on that day the LORD alone will be lifted high.

A day against everything proud

12For the LORD of Armies has set a day against everything proud and towering,
against everything raised high, and it will be brought down,
13against all the cedars of Lebanon, high and towering,
and against all the oaks of Bashan,
14against all the towering mountains,
against all the hills raised high,
15against every tall tower,
against every wall built strong,
16against all the ships of Tarshish,
and against every splendid vessel.
17Humankind’s pride will be bent down,
people’s lofty airs laid low,
and on that day the LORD alone will be lifted high.
18As for the idols, they will be gone, every one.
19People will crawl into caves in the rock and pits in the ground,
away from the dread of the LORD and from his majestic splendor,
when he rises up to make the earth shudder.
20On that day people will fling away their idols of silver and their idols of gold,
made for them to bow down to,
out to the moles and the bats,
21so that they can creep into the cracks of the rocks and the crevices of the crags,
away from the dread of the LORD and from his majestic splendor,
when he rises up to make the earth shudder.
22Have done with humankind, who live by a breath in the nostrils,
for what are they worth?
fields.summary: In days to come the nations will stream to the mountain of God’s house and hammer their swords into plow blades. A day is coming against everything proud, when God alone will be exalted.

fields.title: Isaiah 3
fields.body_html:
Jerusalem stripped of what it leans on

1For look: the Lord, the LORD of Armies, is about to take away from Jerusalem and from Judah everything they lean on,
all the bread they rely on and all the water they rely on,
2the hero and the fighting man,
the judge and the prophet, the fortune-teller and the elder,
3the officer over fifty and the man of high rank,
the adviser, the clever magician, and the expert in spells.
4I will give them boys to be their officials,
and fickle whims will govern them.
5The people will oppress one another,
each person against the next and each against a neighbor.
The young will defy the old,
and the despised will defy the respected.
6One man will catch hold of his brother in their father’s house:
“You still own a cloak. Be our chief,
and let this pile of rubble be in your care.”
7On that day he will raise his voice and say, “I am no binder of wounds!
There is no bread in my house and no cloak.
Do not set me up as the people’s chief.”
8Jerusalem has tripped and Judah lies fallen,
for what they say and what they do opposes the LORD;
they rebel in full view of his glory.
9Their faces give evidence against them.
Like Sodom, they announce their sin openly and do not conceal it.
Woe to their souls! They have dealt out harm to themselves.
10Say of the righteous that good awaits them,
for they will feed on the harvest of what they have done.
11Woe to the wicked! Trouble lies ahead,
for they will get back the same treatment their hands gave.
12My people! Their taskmasters are childish,
and women govern them.
My people, those who guide you lead you off course;
they have swallowed up the road you should walk.

The LORD brings a charge

13The LORD takes his place to bring a charge;
he stands up to judge the peoples.
14The LORD comes into court against the elders and the leaders of his people:
You are the ones who have burned the vineyard;
your houses hold what you robbed from the poor.
15What right do you have to crush my people and to grind the faces of the poor?
declares the Lord GOD of Armies.

The proud daughters of Zion

16The LORD said: Since the daughters of Zion are proud
and go about with heads held high and flirting eyes,
stepping daintily as they walk and jingling the rings on their ankles,
17the Lord will cover the heads of the daughters of Zion with scabs,
and the LORD will strip their foreheads bare.

18On that day the Lord will strip away their finery: the anklets, the headbands, and the moon-shaped ornaments, 19the eardrops, the bracelets, and the veils, 20the headdresses, the ankle chains, the sashes, the vials of perfume, and the amulets, 21the signet rings and the nose rings, 22the festive garments, the outer robes, the wraps, and the money bags, 23the hand mirrors, the linen garments, the turbans, and the long veils.
24Then, where there was perfume, there will be the smell of rot; where there was a belt, a rope; where hair was elegantly arranged, a bare scalp;
where a rich robe was worn, a band of sackcloth;
and a burn scar where there was beauty.
25The sword will cut down your men,
and your mighty ones will fall in war.
26Her gates will moan and grieve,
and she will sit on the ground, emptied of all she had.
fields.summary: God will take away from Jerusalem everything it leans on, and brings a charge against its leaders for crushing the poor. The proud daughters of Zion will lose their finery.

fields.title: Isaiah 4
fields.body_html:
Seven women and one man

1On that day seven women will seize one man and plead,
“We will pay for our own food and our own clothing.
Just let us bear your name, and so remove our shame.”

Beauty and glory for the survivors

2On that day the branch of the LORD will become a thing of beauty and glory, and the fruit of the land will be the boast and the splendor of Israel’s survivors. 3Then those still left in Zion, those remaining in Jerusalem, will be named holy: everyone in Jerusalem who is written down for life. 4This will be when the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and rinsed the bloodguilt of Jerusalem out of her, by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning. 5Then over the whole site of Mount Zion and over those who gather there, the LORD will create a cloud and smoke by day and the shining of a blazing fire by night. Above all the glory a canopy will be spread. 6There will be a booth to give shade from the daytime heat, a place of safety and cover when storm and rain beat down.
fields.summary: Seven women will cling to one man, but the survivors in Zion will be called holy, and God’s glory will shelter them.

fields.title: Isaiah 5
fields.body_html:
A song about my friend’s vineyard

1Let me sing a song for my dear friend, my friend’s song about his vineyard:
My friend owned a vineyard on a hilltop rich in soil.
2He broke up its soil, removed the stones, and set out vines of the finest kind.
He built a tower in the middle of it and also hewed out a wine vat there.
He waited for it to bear grapes, but what it bore was stinking fruit.
3Now then, people of Jerusalem and people of Judah,
be the judges between me and my vineyard.
4What else could I have done for my vineyard that I left undone?
I waited for it to bear grapes; why did it bear stinking ones?
5So now I will let you know what I mean to do to my vineyard:
I will pull up its hedge so that it is grazed bare;
I will knock down its wall so that it is trampled.
6I will lay it waste. No one will prune it or hoe around its vines;
thorns and briers will spring up.
I will even forbid the clouds to drop rain on it.
7The vineyard of the LORD of Armies is the house of Israel,
and the people of Judah are the planting that delighted him.
He waited for justice, but what he found was bloodshed;
for righteousness, but what he heard was a cry of the wronged.

Woe after woe

8Woe to those who buy up house after house and attach field after field,
until no room is left and you are settled all alone in the heart of the land.
9In my hearing the LORD of Armies has sworn:
Many houses will surely be left in ruins, large, fine houses standing empty, with no one to live in them.
10Ten acres of vineyard will yield only about 6 gallons of wine,
and about 6 bushels of seed will produce only about half a bushel of grain.

11Woe to those who get up at dawn to chase after beer,
who linger late into the evening until wine sets them on fire.
12Lyre and harp, tambourine and flute, and wine fill their banquets,
but they pay no attention to what the LORD is doing
and do not notice the work of his hands.
13That is why my people will be carried off into exile, because they do not know.
Their leading men will starve,
and the common crowd will faint from thirst.
14So Sheol has stretched its throat wide and opened its jaws beyond measure,
and down into it go the city’s nobles and its crowds, its noisy throng and all who revel in it.
15So humankind is bowed down, each person is made low,
and proud eyes are cast down.
16But the LORD of Armies stands high in justice,
and the holy God shows that he is holy by acting in righteousness.
17Lambs will graze there as in their own pasture,
and strangers will feed among the ruins of the rich.
18Woe to those who tow their guilt behind them with ropes of falsehood
and haul their sin along as though hitched to a cart.
19They say, “Let him be quick and hurry up with his work, so we can see it!
May the plan of the Holy One of Israel draw near and arrive, so we can know it!”

20Woe to those who name evil as good and good as evil,
who turn darkness into light and light into darkness,
who turn bitter into sweet and sweet into bitter.

21Woe to those who are wise in their own view
and shrewd as they see themselves.
22Woe to the mighty warriors of the wine cup,
the valiant men who excel at blending strong drink,
23who declare the guilty innocent in exchange for a bribe
and rob the righteous of their righteous cause.

Anger that has not turned back

24So, just as flames devour stubble and dry grass collapses into the fire,
their root will turn to rot and their blossom will rise like dust,
because they have thrown away the instruction of the LORD of Armies
and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel.
25That is why the anger of the LORD blazes against his people. He has raised his hand against them and struck them down. The mountains shook,
and their corpses lay like trash in the middle of the streets.
In spite of all this, his anger has not turned back;
his hand is still stretched out.
26He will raise a signal flag for the nations far away and whistle to call them from the ends of the earth.
And see, they come at full speed!
27Among them no one is weary, no one trips; they do not nod off or fall asleep.
No soldier’s belt is untied at the waist, no strap of a sandal snaps.
28Their arrows have keen points, and every bow is drawn back ready.
The hoofs of their horses are counted as hard as flint; the wheels of their chariots whirl like a storm wind.
29The roar they raise is like a lion’s;
they roar like young lions. Growling, they take hold of the prey and drag it away, and there is no one to snatch it back.
30On that day they will growl over their prey like the roaring of the sea.
Look out over the land: there is darkness and distress, and the light has grown dark in its clouds.
fields.summary: Isaiah sings of a vineyard that yielded only bad grapes, a picture of Israel and Judah. Woe after woe is pronounced on the greedy and the corrupt, and God’s anger has not turned back.

fields.title: Isaiah 6
fields.body_html:
The Lord seated on a throne

1In the year King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and towering, and the hem of his robe filled the temple. 2Seraphim stood in attendance over him, and each of them had six wings. With one pair it kept its face covered, with one pair it kept its feet covered, and with one pair it flew.
3And they kept calling to each other,
“Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Armies!
All that fills the earth is his glory.”
4At the sound of the one calling, the bases of the doorways trembled, and smoke filled the temple. 5Then I said, “Woe to me! I am finished. My lips are unclean, and the people I live among have unclean lips, and with my own eyes I have looked on the King, the LORD of Armies!” 6Then one of the seraphim flew to me. In its hand was a glowing coal that it had picked up off the altar with tongs. 7It touched my mouth with it and said, “See, this has touched your lips. Your guilt is removed, and atonement is made for your sin.” 8Then I heard the voice of the Lord asking, “Whom am I to send? Who will go on our behalf?” I answered, “I am ready. Send me.”
9He said, “Go, and say to this people:
‘Hear and hear again, yet do not understand;
look and look again, yet do not come to know.’
10Fatten the heart of this people,
weigh down their ears, and smear their eyes shut,
so that their eyes do not see, their ears do not hear, and their heart does not understand, and they do not turn and find healing.’”
11Then I asked, “How long, Lord?”
He answered, “Until towns lie in ruins with no one living in them, and houses have no one in them,
and the farmland is laid waste and left desolate,
12and the LORD has sent the people far off,
and much of the land lies empty and abandoned.
13Should a tenth still be left in it, that too will go to the fire once more,
like a terebinth or an oak that is felled and leaves only a stump.
But its stump is a holy seed.”
fields.summary: In the year King Uzziah dies, Isaiah sees the Lord seated on a throne, with seraphim calling to each other that God is holy. His lips are cleansed, and he is sent to a people who will not understand.

fields.title: Isaiah 7
fields.body_html:
Two charred ends of firewood

1In the days of Ahaz son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up to Jerusalem to make war on it, but they were not able to take it. 2Word came to the house of David: “Aram has camped in Ephraim.” Then the king’s heart and the hearts of his people shook, like the trees of a forest swaying in the wind. 3The LORD said to Isaiah, “Take your son Shear-jashub and go out to meet Ahaz at the end of the water channel from the Upper Pool, on the road to the Fuller’s Field, 4and say to him, ‘Watch yourself and keep still. Have no fear. Do not let your courage fail because of these two charred ends of firewood, still smoking: the hot anger of Rezin and Aram and the son of Remaliah. 5Aram, along with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has plotted harm against you. They say, 6“Let us march against Judah and fill it with dread. Let us break through its walls and take it for ourselves, and put a king in it: the son of Tabeel.”

7So the Lord GOD says this:
“It will not stand. It will not come about.
8For Aram’s head is Damascus, and Damascus’s head is Rezin.
Within sixty-five years Ephraim will be broken apart and cease to be a people.
9Ephraim’s head is Samaria, and Samaria’s head is the son of Remaliah.
If you do not hold firm in trust, you will not be held firm.”‘”

A sign for Ahaz

10The LORD spoke to Ahaz once more: 11“Ask the LORD your God for a sign. Let your request reach down to the depths or up to the heights above.” 12Ahaz replied, “I will make no request, and I will not test the LORD.” 13Then Isaiah said, “Listen, house of David! Is wearing people out such a small thing to you that you now wear out my God as well? 14Because of this, the Lord himself will give all of you a sign: see, the young woman is pregnant; she will give birth to a son and call him by the name Immanuel. 15Curds and honey will be his food by the time he can turn away from what is bad and choose what is good. 16Even before the boy is able to turn from what is bad and choose what is good, the land of those two kings who frighten you will be abandoned. 17The LORD will bring days on you, on your people, and on your royal house that have not been seen since Ephraim split off from Judah: the king of Assyria!

The fly and the bee

18On that day the LORD will whistle for the fly from the farthest streams of Egypt and for the bee in the land of Assyria. 19They will all swarm in and settle in the gorges under the cliffs and in the cracks of the rocks, on every thorny shrub and at every place where the flocks drink. 20On that day the Lord will shave with a hired razor from beyond the Euphrates, the king of Assyria. He will shave the head and the hair of the body, and it will strip away the beard as well.

21On that day someone will keep a heifer and two sheep alive. 22They will give so much milk that he will have curds to eat; indeed, curds and honey will be the food of all who are left in the land. 23On that day every vineyard of a thousand vines, worth a thousand pieces of silver, will be overrun by thorns and briers. 24Anyone who goes there will carry a bow and arrows, for thorns and briers will cover the whole land. 25As for the hills that used to be worked with the hoe, you will not go to them for fear of the thorns and briers. Oxen will be let out to graze there, and sheep will trample the ground.”
fields.summary: When Aram and Israel threaten Judah, Isaiah tells Ahaz not to fear these two charred ends of firewood. God offers a sign: the young woman will give birth to a son and call him Immanuel.

fields.title: Isaiah 8
fields.body_html:
Maher-shalal-hash-baz

1The LORD said to me, “Get yourself a large tablet and write on it in ordinary letters, ‘Belonging to Maher-shalal-hash-baz.’ 2I will have trustworthy witnesses confirm it for me, Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Jeberekiah.” 3I went in to the prophetess, and she became pregnant and bore a son. Then the LORD said to me, “Give him the name Maher-shalal-hash-baz. 4For before the child can say ‘Father’ or ‘Mother,’ the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria will be hauled away before the king of Assyria.”

5The LORD spoke to me once more:
6“This people has turned away from the gently flowing waters of Shiloah
and takes delight in Rezin and the son of Remaliah.
7So now the Lord is about to bring against them the waters of the River, strong and plentiful:
the king of Assyria and all his glory.
It will rise over all its channels and spill over all its banks.
8It will surge on into Judah, flooding and passing through until it reaches the neck.
Its outspread wings will cover the whole width of your land, O Immanuel.”

9Do your worst, you peoples, and be shattered!
Listen, all you distant lands!
Arm for war, and be shattered;
arm for war, and be shattered!
10Draw up your plans; they will be undone.
Give the order; it will not stand. For God is with us.

Fear only the LORD of Armies

11For this is what the LORD said to me while his hand held me hard, warning me not to follow the way of this people:
12“Do not call something a plot just because this people calls it a plot.
What frightens them must not frighten you; do not tremble at it.
13The LORD of Armies is the one you must treat as holy.
Let him be the one you fear, let him be the one who makes you tremble.
14He will be a holy place of refuge,
but also a stone that people strike against and a rock they trip over, for both houses of Israel; a trap and a snare for those who live in Jerusalem.
15Many will stumble on them and fall;
they will be broken, caught in the snare, and carried off.”

16Wrap up the testimony,
and put a seal on the instruction among my disciples.
17I will wait on the LORD while he keeps his face hidden from the house of Jacob;
I will look to him in hope.
18Here I am with the children the LORD has given me. We are signs and omens in Israel
from the LORD of Armies, who makes his home on Mount Zion.

To the instruction and the testimony

19When they tell you, “Seek out the ghosts and the familiar spirits that chirp and moan,”
should a people not seek its own God?
Should they go to the dead on behalf of the living?
20To the instruction and the testimony!
Those who do not speak in keeping with this word have no dawn before them.
21They will roam through the land, worn down and hungry.
When hunger gnaws at them, they will rage and curse their king and their God, and turn their faces upward.
22They will stare at the ground,
and there will be trouble and darkness, the dimness of anguish; into thick darkness they are driven.
fields.summary: Isaiah’s son is named Maher-shalal-hash-baz as a sign that Assyria will come. The people must fear only God and turn to the instruction and the testimony.

fields.title: Isaiah 9
fields.body_html:
A great light for those in the dark

1Yet the land in anguish will not be left in gloom. At first he brought low the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but afterward he will bring honor to the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations.
2The people walking in the dark have seen a great light.
Those who lived in a land as dark as death now have light shining on them.
3You have made the nation grow and filled it with great joy.
In your presence they are glad with the gladness of harvest time,
the delight of those who share out the spoils of war.
4For you have smashed the yoke that weighed them down,
the pole pressing on their shoulders, the rod of the man who drove them,
as on the day of Midian.
5For every boot that stamped and thundered in battle,
every cloak caked in blood,
will go to be burned, food for the fire.
6For a child has been born for us, a son has been given to us,
and the right to rule rests on his shoulders.
He has been named Planner of Wonders, God the Mighty Warrior,
Father for All Time, Ruler of Peace.
7His rule will grow and grow, and its peace will never end, on David’s throne and over his kingdom,
as he makes it firm and holds it up with justice and righteousness
from now on and for all time.
The burning zeal of the LORD of Armies will make this happen.

A word sent against Jacob

8The Lord has sent out a word against Jacob,
and it has come down on Israel.
9Every one of them will find it out,
Ephraim and everyone living in Samaria,
the people who boast with proud, swollen hearts,
10“Brick has tumbled down, but we will build in cut stone;
sycamore wood has been chopped down,
but cedar will take its place.”
11So the LORD has raised Rezin’s foes high against them
and spurred on their enemies:
12Aram from the east and the Philistines from the west
have gulped Israel down with greedy mouths.
In spite of all this, his anger has not turned back,
and his hand is still stretched out.
13And still the people have not come back to the one who struck them,
nor gone looking for the LORD of Armies.

14So in one day the LORD lopped off Israel’s head and tail, the tall palm and the lowly rush.
15The head means the old men and the people of high standing;
the tail means the prophet whose teaching is false.
16Those who steer this people lead them off course,
and those they steer are swallowed up.
17That is why the Lord takes no delight in its young men and shows no mercy to its orphans and widows.
Every one of them is godless and does evil,
and every mouth speaks shameful folly.
In spite of all this, his anger has not turned back,
and his hand is still stretched out.
18Wickedness blazes up like a fire.
It eats through thorn and brier,
catches the tangled undergrowth of the forest,
and sends it whirling skyward in towering smoke.
19The fury of the LORD of Armies has burned the land black,
and the people have become like wood for the fire.
No one spares even his own brother.
20They tear at food to their right and stay hungry;
they gulp it down to their left and are never filled.
Every one of them feeds on his own arm.
21Manasseh preys on Ephraim, Ephraim on Manasseh,
and both join hands against Judah.
In spite of all this, his anger has not turned back,
and his hand is still stretched out.
fields.summary: The people walking in the dark have seen a great light, for a child is born who will reign on David’s throne forever. Yet God’s anger against Israel’s pride has not turned back.

fields.title: Isaiah 10
fields.body_html:
Woe to those who write wicked statutes

1Woe to those who make wicked statutes,
and to the scribes who keep writing out misery,
2to push the needy away from a fair hearing
and strip the poor among my people of their rights,
so that widows become their spoil
and orphans their loot.
3What will you do on the day you are called to account,
when ruin comes sweeping in from far away?
Whom will you flee to for help?
And where will you leave your wealth behind?
4Nothing is left but to crouch down among the captives
or to fall among the dead.
Even so, his anger has not turned back;
his hand is still stretched out.

Assyria, the rod of my anger

5Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger!
The club they hold in their hand is my indignation.
6I send him against a corrupt nation;
against the people who stir my wrath I give him orders,
to carry off spoil and haul away plunder,
and to stamp them into the ground like mud in the streets.
7But that is not what he has in view;
that is not the plan in his heart.
What he has at heart is to wipe out and cut down nations, and not a few.
8For he says,
“My commanders, are they not kings, every one of them?
9Did Calno not go the way of Carchemish?
Did Hamath not go the way of Arpad,
and Samaria the way of Damascus?
10Just as my hand laid hold of kingdoms full of idols,
whose carved images outnumbered those of Jerusalem and Samaria,
11what I did to Samaria and its idols,
will I not do the same to Jerusalem and its images?”

12When the Lord has completed everything he is doing on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem,
I will punish what has grown from the swollen pride of the king of Assyria,
and the glory of his haughty look.
13For he says, “My own strong hand has done this,
and my wisdom, for I am shrewd.
I wiped away the borders between peoples and stripped their storehouses bare;
like a mighty bull I toppled those who sat on thrones.
14My hand found the riches of the peoples as easily as a bird’s nest;
the way someone collects eggs that have been deserted,
I collected the whole earth.
No wing fluttered; no beak opened; no peep was heard.”
15Can an ax take pride over the one who chops with it,
or a saw make itself greater than the one who works it?
That would be like a stick swinging the hands that lift it,
or a wooden club lifting someone who is not wood!
16So the Lord GOD of Armies will send a wasting disease into his well-fed troops,
and beneath his splendor a blaze will flare up like a burning fire.
17The one who is Israel’s Light will turn to fire,
its Holy One to flame;
it will flare up and burn up his thornbushes and briers, all in a single day.
18The splendor of his forest and his orchard land it will wipe out, body and soul,
and it will be as the strength drains out of a sick man.
19What is left of the trees in his forest will be so few
that a child could list them.

A remnant will return

20On that day the remnant of Israel, those of the house of Jacob who have escaped,
will no longer lean on the one who struck them down.
Their support will be the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in all faithfulness.
21A remnant will return, Jacob’s remnant,
to the Mighty God.
22Even if your people, Israel, are as many as the grains of sand by the sea,
only a remnant within them will return.
An end has been decided, and it comes flooding in with justice.
23For the Lord GOD of Armies
is about to bring a full and settled end within the whole land.

24Therefore the Lord GOD of Armies says this:
Do not fear Assyria, my people who live in Zion.
He strikes you with the rod
and raises his staff over you the way Egypt did.
25For only a little while longer,
and the fury will be spent;
then my anger will turn to their ruin.
26The LORD of Armies will crack a whip over him,
as in the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb.
His staff will be over the sea,
and he will lift it up as he did in Egypt.
27On that day the load he laid on your shoulder will be taken away,
and his yoke off your neck.
The yoke will snap because of fatness.
28He has reached Aiath and marched through Migron;
at Michmash he leaves his baggage.
29They have gone across the pass:
“Geba will be our camp for the night!”
Ramah is trembling;
Gibeah of Saul has taken flight.
30Raise your voice and cry, Daughter Gallim!
Take heed, Laishah! Afflicted Anathoth!
31Madmenah has run away;
those who live in Gebim have hurried their goods to safety.
32Before this day is over he will stand at Nob,
waving his fist toward the mountain of Daughter Zion,
toward Jerusalem’s hill.

33Look! The Lord GOD of Armies is about to strip away the boughs with a terrifying crash.
The trees that tower highest will be cut down;
the proud heights will be laid low.
34He will hack down the tangled forest with iron,
and Lebanon will come crashing down by a mighty one.
fields.summary: Woe to those who write unjust laws. Assyria is the rod of God’s anger but will itself be judged, and a remnant of Israel will return.

fields.title: Isaiah 11
fields.body_html:
A shoot from Jesse’s stump

1A shoot will grow from Jesse’s stump,
and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.
2The Spirit of the LORD will settle on him:
the Spirit who gives wisdom and insight, the Spirit of counsel and power,
the Spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD.
3Fearing the LORD will be his delight.
He will not judge by what his eyes take in,
or give rulings by what reaches his ears.
4He will do right by the poor when he judges,
and give fair rulings for the lowly of the land.
With his word as a rod he will strike the earth;
the breath from his lips will bring death to the wicked.
5Righteousness will be the belt around his waist,
and faithfulness the sash bound at his hips.
6The wolf will stay as a guest with the lamb,
and the leopard will lie down beside the young goat;
calf and young lion and fatted steer will be together,
and a small boy will drive them along.
7Cow and bear will feed side by side,
their young will rest together,
and the lion will eat straw as the ox does.
8A baby still at the breast will play by the cobra’s hole,
and a child just weaned will reach into the viper’s den.
9None will hurt and none will destroy anywhere on my holy mountain,
for the earth will be as full of knowing the LORD
as the sea is full of water.

A rallying flag for the peoples

10On that day the root of Jesse will stand as a rallying flag for the peoples.
Nations will turn to him for guidance,
and the place where he settles will be filled with glory.

11On that day the Lord will act again with his own hand, a second time,
to win back the remnant of his people who are left:
from Assyria and from Egypt, from Pathros and Cush, from Elam, Shinar, and Hamath,
and from the coastlands of the sea.
12He will hoist a flag as a signal to the nations.
Those driven out of Israel he will gather in,
and those of Judah who were scattered he will bring together
from the four corners of the earth.
13Ephraim’s envy will vanish,
and Judah’s adversaries will be cut off.
Ephraim will no longer envy Judah,
and Judah will no longer treat Ephraim as an enemy.
14They will swoop down on the slopes of Philistia to the west;
together they will plunder the peoples of the east.
Edom and Moab will be within their grasp,
and the Ammonites will obey them.
15The LORD will destroy the gulf of the Egyptian sea;
he will sweep his hand over the River with his scorching wind
and break it into seven streams,
so that people can cross in their sandals.
16A highway will lead out of Assyria for the remnant of his people who are left there,
as one did for Israel
on the day they came up out of the land of Egypt.
fields.summary: A shoot will come from the stump of Jesse, and the Spirit of God will rest on him; he will judge the poor with justice, and the wolf will live with the lamb. God will gather the scattered people.

fields.title: Isaiah 12
fields.body_html:
A song for that day

1On that day you will say:
LORD, I thank you! You were angry with me,
but your anger has turned back, and now you comfort me.
2Look, God is my salvation! I will rely on him and not be afraid.
For Yah, the LORD, is my strength and my song;
he has become my salvation.
3Rejoicing, you will draw water
from the springs of salvation.
4On that day you will say:
Give thanks to the LORD; call on his name!
Make his deeds known among the peoples;
remind them that his name is lifted high.
5Make music to the LORD, for he has acted in majesty;
let the whole earth come to know it.
6Raise the cry and sing out, you who live in Zion,
for the Holy One of Israel, who is among you, is great.
fields.summary: On that day the people will sing that God is their salvation and draw water from the wells of salvation.

fields.title: Isaiah 13
fields.body_html:
The oracle about Babylon

1The oracle about Babylon that Isaiah son of Amoz saw.
2Hoist a signal flag on a bare hilltop;
shout out to them;
wave them on,
so they march in through the gates of the nobles.
3I myself have given orders to my consecrated troops;
I have called up my warriors to carry out my anger,
those who exult in my majesty.
4Hear the roar on the mountains, like a vast multitude!
Hear the din of kingdoms, of nations assembling!
the LORD of Armies is gathering an army for war.
5They come from a faraway land, from the ends of the sky:
the LORD and the weapons of his fury,
to ruin the whole earth.
6Howl, for the day of the LORD is close at hand!
It will come like ruin from the Almighty.
7So every hand will hang helpless,
and the heart of every mortal will melt.
8They will be filled with dread; cramps and pains will take hold of them;
they will writhe like a woman in labor.
They will stare at one another in shock,
their faces flushed like fire.
9Look, the day of the LORD is on its way,
merciless, full of fury and blazing anger,
to turn the earth into a wasteland;
and he will wipe out the sinners who live in it.
10The stars of the sky and their constellations will not send out their light;
the sun will be darkened as it comes up,
and the moon will not let its light shine.
11I will call the world to account for its evil
and the wicked for their guilt.
I will end the pride of the arrogant
and bring down the haughtiness of tyrants.
12I will make human beings harder to find than refined gold,
and mortals scarcer than gold from Ophir.
13So I will make the sky shudder,
and the earth will be jolted out of its place
by the fury of the LORD of Armies,
on the day his anger blazes.
14Like a gazelle being chased,
like sheep that no one rounds up,
they will each turn back to their own people and run off,
each one to their own country.
15Anyone who is found will be run through,
and anyone who is seized will be cut down by the sword.
16Before their eyes their little children will be smashed;
their houses will be looted
and their wives raped.
17Look, I am rousing the Medes to attack them,
a people who count silver as nothing
and care nothing for gold.
18Their bows will strike down the young men;
they will show no mercy to newborn babies,
and they will look on children without pity.
19Babylon, the gem among kingdoms,
the splendor the Chaldeans are so proud of,
will become what Sodom and Gomorrah became when God overturned them.
20No one will ever live there again or settle there, from one generation to the next.
No Arab will set up a tent there,
and no shepherds will bed down their flocks there.
21Desert beasts will make their dens there instead;
screeching creatures will crowd the houses.
Ostriches will settle there,
and wild goats will prance there.
22Hyenas will call to one another in its fortresses,
and jackals in its luxurious palaces.
Its hour has nearly come;
its days will not be drawn out.
fields.summary: Isaiah’s oracle against Babylon announces the day of God, when the Medes will overthrow the city.

fields.title: Isaiah 14
fields.body_html:
Jacob shown mercy

1Yes, the LORD will show mercy to Jacob. He will choose Israel once more and let them settle in peace on their own soil. The foreigner living among them will join them, and such people will bind themselves to the house of Jacob. 2Peoples will take them and bring them home, and the house of Israel will hold those peoples as their own, male and female servants on the land of the LORD. Those who once carried them off will become their captives, and they will rule over those who oppressed them.

A mocking song about the king of Babylon

3And on the day when the LORD gives you rest from your sorrow and your unrest, and from the cruel bondage forced on you,
4you will sing this mocking song about the king of Babylon:
How still the oppressor has become!
How his raging has come to an end!
5The LORD has snapped the rod of the wicked,
the scepter held by tyrants,
6the rod that beat the peoples in fury with blow after blow that never let up,
that ruled the nations in anger
and hunted them down with no one to hold it back.
7Now all the earth lies still and calm;
people burst out in shouts of joy.
8Even the junipers and the cedars of Lebanon are glad over you:
“Ever since you lay down, no one climbs up here to chop us down.”
9Down below, Sheol is astir because of you, waiting to meet you as you arrive.
It wakes the dead for your sake, all who once led the earth;
it makes every king of the nations rise from his throne.
10They will all speak up and say to you,
“So you too have been brought low, as weak as we are! Now you are one of us!”
11Your splendor has gone down to Sheol, along with the music of your harps.
Under you a mattress of maggots is spread, and worms are your blanket.
12How you have fallen from the heavens, shining one, son of Dawn!
You have been hewn down to the earth, you who brought the nations to their knees!
13In your heart you said, “I will climb into the heavens
and lift my throne higher than the stars of God.
I will take my seat on the mountain where the assembly meets, in the far heights of Zaphon.
14I will rise higher than the cloud tops;
I will make myself the equal of the Most High.”
15Instead you are dragged down to Sheol, into the deepest corners of the pit.
16All who see you will gaze at you and look you over closely:
“Can this be the man who set the earth trembling
and made kingdoms quake,
17who turned the world into a wasteland and pulled down its cities,
who never set his prisoners free to go home?”
18Every king of the nations, every one of them,
lies at rest with honor, each in a tomb of his own,
19But you have been flung away from your grave like a branch nobody wants,
dressed in the bodies of the slain, of those run through by the sword,
who sink down to the stones of the pit, like a corpse that feet have trampled.
20You will have no share with them in a grave,
because you ruined your own land and put your own people to death.
The descendants of evildoers will never again be spoken of.
21Make ready a place to slaughter his sons for the guilt of their fathers,
so that they never rise up to take over the earth
and crowd the whole world with their cities.
22I will rise against them, declares the LORD of Armies.
I will wipe out Babylon’s name and every survivor, its children and its children’s children, declares the LORD.
23I will turn it into a home for hedgehogs and a land of marshy pools,
and I will sweep it clean with destruction as with a broom, declares the LORD of Armies.

Assyria broken and Philistia warned

24The LORD of Armies has taken an oath:
What I have had in mind will surely happen;
what I have decided will stand firm,
25to shatter Assyria in my own land
and trample it on my mountains.
Its yoke will be lifted off them,
and its load will slip from their shoulders.
26This is the purpose decided for the whole world,
and this is the hand stretched out over every nation.
27The LORD of Armies has made up his mind; who can overturn it?
His hand is outstretched; who can pull it back?

28In the year of King Ahaz’s death, this oracle came:
29Philistia, do not celebrate, any of you,
because the stick that beat you has been snapped.
Out of the snake’s root a viper will spring up,
and what it bears will be a winged fiery serpent.
30The very poorest will have pasture to feed on,
and the needy will rest in safety.
But I will make your root die of hunger,
and what is left of you it will kill.
31Gate, howl! City, cry for help!
All Philistia, you are melting in fear!
Smoke is pouring down from the north,
and no one in its ranks lags behind.
32What reply should be given to the envoys of that nation?
This: The LORD has laid the foundation of Zion,
and the downtrodden among his people will find shelter in her.
fields.summary: God will have mercy on Jacob, and Israel will mock the fallen king of Babylon, the shining one, son of Dawn, hewn down to the earth. Assyria will be broken and Philistia is warned.

fields.title: Isaiah 15
fields.body_html:
The oracle concerning Moab

1The oracle concerning Moab.
In a single night Ar of Moab is stripped bare and silenced;
in a single night Kir of Moab is stripped bare and silenced.
2Up to the temple they go, and Dibon to the high places, to weep;
for Nebo and for Medeba Moab wails.
Every head among them is bald, every beard clipped short.
3They have tied sackcloth on in its streets;
on its roofs and in its open squares the whole people wails, dissolving in tears.
4Heshbon raises a cry, and Elealeh with it;
the sound carries as far as Jahaz.
That is why Moab’s soldiers shout in alarm,
and Moab shudders to the depths of its being.
5My heart cries out for Moab;
those fleeing from it reach Zoar and Eglath-shelishiyah.
Up the climb to Luhith they go, weeping all the way;
along the road to Horonaim they lift a cry of disaster.
6The waters of Nimrim have turned to waste ground.
The grass has dried out, the fresh shoots have failed,
and not a green thing remains.
7That is why they haul away the riches they had amassed
and the goods they had laid by,
across the Wadi of the Poplars.
8A cry runs all around the borders of Moab;
the wailing is heard at Eglaim,
the wailing is heard at Beer-elim.
9The waters of Dimon are filled with blood,
and I will add yet more to Dimon’s troubles:
a lion against the survivors of Moab,
against whoever is left in the land.
fields.summary: Isaiah’s oracle laments the destruction of Moab.

fields.title: Isaiah 16
fields.body_html:
Moab’s outcasts seek shelter

1Send the ruler of the land his lamb, from Sela through the wilderness
to the mountain of Daughter Zion.
2Like birds darting here and there, like nestlings thrown out,
the daughters of Moab will be at the crossings of the Arnon.
3Offer counsel; give a ruling.
Let your shade at midday be as dark as night.
Shelter the outcasts; do not give away the one who flees.
4Let my outcasts from Moab stay among you as guests;
be a shelter for them from the destroyer.
For the oppressor will be gone, the ruin will stop,
and those who trample others will vanish from the land.
5A throne will be made secure by loyal love,
and a ruler will take his seat on it faithfully, in David’s tent.
He will judge, he will search out justice, and he will be quick to act in righteousness.
6We have heard of Moab’s pride, proud beyond measure:
its haughty airs, its pride, its overbearing fury. Its big talk comes to nothing.

Weeping for the vine of Sibmah

7So Moab will wail, Moab for itself, all of it wailing;
you will moan, crushed and broken, for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth.
8The terraces of Heshbon wilt, and the vine of Sibmah with them; the masters of the nations have beaten down its choicest stems,
stems that once stretched to Jazer and wandered into the wilderness,
whose runners spread out and crossed the sea.
9That is why I weep along with Jazer for the vine of Sibmah;
my tears pour over you, Heshbon and Elealeh,
for the glad shout over your ripe fruit and your harvest has died away.
10Gladness and delight are gathered up and gone from the garden land.
In the vineyards there is no singing and no cheering;
the treader treads no wine in the winepresses. I have silenced the harvest shout.
11So deep within me I moan for Moab like a plucked lyre,
and my inmost being moans for Kir-heres.
12Moab will come before its god and tire itself out at the high place;
it will go into its sanctuary to pray, and it will accomplish nothing.
13Such was the word the LORD spoke about Moab in earlier days. 14But now the LORD has spoken: Within three years, counted as a hired worker counts them, the glory of Moab with all its great throng will be treated as nothing, and those left over will be a handful, without strength.
fields.summary: Moab’s outcasts seek shelter in Zion, and the prophet weeps for the vine of Sibmah.

fields.title: Isaiah 17
fields.body_html:
Damascus and Ephraim brought low

1The oracle concerning Damascus.
Look, Damascus is soon to be a city no more;
it will become a heap of fallen stones.
2Aroer’s towns stand empty
and are given over to flocks;
the sheep will rest there, and nobody will drive them off.
3The stronghold will vanish from Ephraim
and royal rule from Damascus;
Aram’s survivors will end up like the glory of the Israelites,
declares the LORD of Armies.

4On that day Jacob’s glory will dwindle,
and his sleek body will grow thin.
5It will be like a reaper sweeping up the standing grain,
his arm cutting the heads of grain,
or like someone picking up stray heads in the Valley of Rephaim.
6Some gleanings will remain in it, like olives left after a tree is beaten:
two or three up in the crown,
four or five out on the branches that bore the crop,
declares the LORD, the God of Israel.

Looking to their Maker

7On that day people will lift their gaze to their Maker,
and their eyes will be on the Holy One of Israel.
8They will no longer look to the altars their own hands built,
or pay attention to what their fingers made,
the Asherah poles and the incense altars.
9On that day their strongholds will be like the deserted sites in the woods and on the hilltops
that the old inhabitants left behind before the Israelites;
the whole land will be a waste.
10You have forgotten the God of your salvation;
the Rock who shelters you has slipped from your mind.
So you lay out lovely gardens
and plant them with cuttings from a foreign vine.
11On the day you plant, you make it grow;
by morning you make your seed burst into bloom;
but the harvest slips away on a day of sickness and pain past all cure.

The roaring nations driven off

12Woe to the din of many peoples,
who roar like the roaring of the seas,
and to the clamor of nations,
who crash like mighty waters crashing!
13The nations thunder like vast waters crashing,
yet at his rebuke they scatter into the distance,
blown away like husks from the hilltops in the wind,
like a swirl of dust in a storm.
14When evening comes, there is sudden dread;
by daybreak they have vanished.
Such is the share of those who loot us,
the fate allotted to those who strip us bare.
fields.summary: Damascus and Ephraim will be brought low, and people will look to their Maker. The roaring nations will be driven off like chaff.

fields.title: Isaiah 18
fields.body_html:
Envoys from beyond the rivers of Cush

1Woe to the land of buzzing wings,
the land that lies beyond the rivers of Cush,
2which dispatches envoys on the sea, in papyrus craft skimming the water.
Go, you swift messengers, to a nation of tall people with smooth skin,
a people dreaded near and far,
a nation of immense strength that treads others down,
whose land is cut through by rivers.
3Everyone who lives in the world, all who make their home on the earth:
when the signal flag goes up on the mountains, you will see it;
when the ram’s horn blasts, you will hear it.

4For the LORD said this to me:
I will keep still and watch from the place where I dwell,
silent as heat glimmering in the sunlight,
as a dew cloud in the warmth of harvest.
5For before the harvest, once the budding is done
and the flower is swelling into a grape that ripens,
he will slice off the new growth with pruning knives
and hack away the trailing branches, clearing them off.
6All of them will be abandoned to the birds of prey on the hills
and to the wild beasts of the land.
The birds of prey will pass the summer on them,
and every wild beast of the land will pass the winter on them.
7At that time gifts will be brought to the LORD of Armies, from a people who are tall with smooth skin, from a people dreaded near and far, a nation of immense strength that treads others down, whose land is cut through by rivers. They will be brought to Mount Zion, the place that bears the name of the LORD of Armies.
fields.summary: Envoys come from beyond the rivers of Cush, and a gift will be brought to God on Mount Zion.

fields.title: Isaiah 19
fields.body_html:
An oracle about Egypt

1An oracle about Egypt.
Look, the LORD is riding a swift cloud, on his way to Egypt.
Egypt’s idols will shake at his coming,
and Egypt’s courage will melt away inside it.
2I will set Egyptians against Egyptians.
They will fight one another, brother with brother and neighbor with neighbor,
city with city and kingdom with kingdom.
3Egypt’s spirit will drain away within it,
and I will throw its plans into confusion.
They will turn for answers to idols and ghosts,
to mediums and to those who consult spirits.
4I will give Egypt into the grip of a hard master;
a strong king will reign over them,
declares the Lord, the LORD of Armies.
5The water will drain from the sea,
and the river will shrink and run dry.
6The canals will reek,
the branches of the Nile in Egypt will run low and dry up,
and the reeds and rushes will waste away.
7The bare banks beside the Nile, at the mouth of the Nile,
and every field sown along the Nile will dry out, blow away, and be gone.
8The fishermen will moan and grieve,
all who drop a hook into the Nile,
and those who spread their nets over the water will lose heart.
9The workers who comb flax will be put to shame,
along with the weavers of white linen.
10Its pillars will be broken,
and all who work for hire will be sick at heart.
11Zoan’s officials are complete fools;
the wisest men who advise Pharaoh offer witless counsel.
How can you tell Pharaoh, “I come from a line of wise men, from kings of long ago”?
12So where are your wise men?
Let them explain to you,
if they know, what the LORD of Armies intends for Egypt.
13Zoan’s officials have played the fool,
and those of Memphis are deluded.
The ones who should be the cornerstone of its tribes have sent Egypt off course.
14The LORD has poured into it a spirit that twists everything,
and they have sent Egypt reeling in all it does,
like a drunk who slips in his own vomit.
15Nothing that Egypt does will succeed,
whether done by head or tail, by palm branch or reed.

16On that day Egypt will be like women, trembling and shaking in fear when the LORD of Armies raises his hand and waves it over them. 17Egypt will come to fear the land of Judah. Each time someone speaks its name, Egyptians will shudder at the plan that the LORD of Armies is making against them.

Egypt will know the LORD

18On that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and bind themselves by oath to the LORD of Armies. One will be known as the City of Destruction.

19On that day an altar to the LORD will stand in the middle of the land of Egypt, and a sacred pillar for the LORD near its border. 20These will stand as a sign and a testimony to the LORD of Armies in the land of Egypt.
